title: Nice to meet you in Cairo
goal: Greet people, give your name, ask how someone is — and swallow three surprises at once: ج pronounced as g, ق turning into a catch in the throat, and question words placed at the very end of the sentence.
bekal: greet and answer greetings like an Egyptian, not like a Fusha textbook
ask someone's name and how they are, using the right form for a man or a woman
build complete sentences without a single verb

dialogs.title: حوار — أول يوم في المعهد
dialogs.intro: It's Budi's first day at a language institute in Dokki, Cairo. He's sitting in the waiting room, and a young Egyptian man sits down next to him.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: And upon you be peace and God's mercy.
lines.literal: and upon-you(pl) the-peace and mercy God.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لأ، أنا مش مصري. أنا من إندونيسيا.
lines.baca: la’, ana mish maṣri. ana min Indunisya.
lines.id: No, I'm not Egyptian. I'm from Indonesia.
lines.literal: no, I not Egyptian. I from Indonesia.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: My name is Budi. And you?

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.id: I'm Ahmad. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: The pleasure is mine. How are you?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أيوه، أنا طالب جديد في المعهد.
lines.id: Yes, I'm a new student at the institute.
lines.literal: yes, I student new in the-institute.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.id: Great! Your Arabic is really good.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.text: معلش، شوية شوية. أهلاً بيك في مصر!
lines.baca: ma‘lesh, shuwayya shuwayya. ahlan biik fi Maṣr!
lines.id: No worries, little by little. Welcome to Egypt!
lines.literal: never-mind, little little. welcome with-you in Egypt!

notes: **A greeting for any time of day.** السلام عليكم is used morning, noon, and night, to one person or a hundred, at the office or at a street stall. In Egypt it's not just a religious greeting but a perfectly normal everyday one, and answering it isn't optional — it's a social duty.

**The letter ج is a hard g — surprise number one.** جميل is not *jamiil* but *gamiil*. جديد is not *jadiid* but *gidiid*. This applies to every word, without exception, across northern Egypt — including Cairo and Alexandria. Once your ear accepts it, half of all Egyptian songs suddenly become easy to follow.

**The letter ق turns into a catch in the throat.** The ’ sign in the pronunciation marks a short break, like the one in the middle of "uh-oh". So لأ is read *la’* and أوي is read *’awi*. The word قهوة, which you may know as *qahwah*, sounds like *’ahwa* in Cairo.

**Question words go at the end of the sentence, not the front.** اسمك إيه؟ is literally "your name what?" This isn't casual style — it's the only correct word order in Egyptian. Putting إيه at the front sounds as odd as saying "What your name is?" in English.

**The word مش negates everything that isn't a verb.** أنا مش مصري = "I'm not Egyptian". One word for every job: مش طالب، مش كويس، مش هنا. Compare that with Fusha, which uses لَيْسَ with all its changing forms — and be grateful.

**The word حضرتك is the Egyptian polite "you".** Use it with older people, officials, people you've just met, and anyone you want to show respect to. The feminine form is also written حضرتك, but read *haḍritik*. Using it is never wrong; leaving it out can sometimes come across as a little rude.

**Two Egyptian words you'll hear every day.** معلش *ma‘lesh* smooths over every small thing that goes wrong — from spilled coffee to a late train. And شوية شوية *shuwayya shuwayya* means "little by little": it's the standard reply to a foreigner apologizing for their broken Arabic.

grammars.title: Sentences without a verb — and without "is"
body: This is the first sentence type you need to master, and the biggest lesson lies in what does NOT appear in it.
after: The pattern: **[what you're talking about] + [what you say about it]**. That's it. Nothing goes in between — no "am", "is" or "are".

Notice there's no "a" either. أنا طالب can mean "I'm a student" or "I'm the student" depending on context — Egyptian doesn't mark it, and the Fusha tanween ٌ ـ that used to do the job has vanished completely.
To negate it, just put مش in front of the second part. A verb, كان, only shows up for the past — but that's for unit 14.

grammars.title: One word, two forms: masculine and feminine
body: Almost every Egyptian greeting has two forms, and the only difference is the last vowel. English "you" doesn't change at all, so this is the mistake English speakers make most often.
after: Look at the middle rows of the table: the spelling is exactly the same, only the pronunciation changes. That's why this book always gives the pronunciation — without vowel marks, the eye can't see the difference, while the ear hears it right away.
The easy rule: **ـك is read -ak to a man and -ik to a woman**. Picking the wrong one isn't dangerous and won't offend anyone, but it instantly marks you as a beginner.

blocks.text: Notice that a morning greeting isn't answered by repeating it. صباح الخير ("morning of goodness") is answered with صباح النور ("morning of light"), and Egyptians love to raise the stakes with صباح الفل ("morning of jasmine") and then صباح القشطة ("morning of cream"). Answering with exactly the same phrase marks you as a foreigner straight away.

blocks.title: When to use the Islamic greeting, and when a neutral one
items: The phrase السلام عليكم is the most common greeting in Egypt, including at the office, on TV, and between strangers. It's a normal everyday greeting, not a sign of piety.
Egypt has millions of Coptic Christians, and with someone you know isn't Muslim, the neutral greeting that's always safe is صباح الخير or أهلاً. Both are polite and carry no religious weight.
Handshakes are common between men and between women. Between a man and a woman, wait for the other person to offer their hand first — customs vary from family to family.

sections.title: Lifesaver phrases for your first day

blocks.text: These phrases are given whole, before you understand how they're built. Learn each one as a single chunk — the breakdown comes in later units.

The phrase مش فاهم has a feminine form, مش فاهمة *mish fahma*, and a plural, مش فاهمين *mish fahmiin*. This three-form pattern will keep coming back; from now on, every time you meet an adjective, get into the habit of asking yourself what its feminine form is.

items: Good morning! What's your name? (to a man)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right possessive ending.
You're in the following situations. Write one suitable sentence in Egyptian Arabic.
items: You walk into a bakery at 8:00 in the morning and greet the baker.
You didn't catch what he said and ask him to repeat it.
You want to ask where the restroom is.
You say goodbye and promise to come back tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: صباح الخير! اسمك إيه؟ — اسمي بودي. — أنا طالب جديد. — إزيك؟ — الحمد لله، كويسة.
اسمي — اسمك — إزيك — أهلاً بيكي — حضرتك
صباح الخير. — صباح النور. — تاني، من فضلك. — الحمام فين، لو سمحت؟ — مع السلامة، أشوفك بكرة.
أنا طالب جديد. — اسمك إيه؟ — اسمي بودي. — أنا مش مصري. — أنا من إندونيسيا.
